title: Schedule Management
sequence: Planning. The schedule is built from the scope baseline, resource information and estimates; Monitor and Control Schedule then runs through Executing and Monitoring & Controlling.

html:
1Core Concepts and Definitions

Purpose of the domain: a plan showing how and when the project delivers the scope, which also serves to communicate, manage stakeholder expectations, report performance and spot delays and risks early.

Term Meaning
Schedule model A representation of the plan for executing the activities (durations, dependencies and other planning data) used to produce the project schedule
Project schedule The output of the schedule model: linked activities with planned dates, durations, milestones and resources; flexible throughout the project to reflect what is learned
Schedule baseline The approved version of a schedule model, changeable only through formal change control and used to compare actual results. Change control is more rigid in predictive work and more flexible, or even absent, in adaptive work
Milestone / milestone list A significant point or event with zero duration; the list says whether each is mandatory (for example contractual) or optional
Effort The number of labor units needed (person-hours, days, weeks)
Duration The number of work periods needed to complete an activity with the estimated resources
Actual duration Calendar time from the actual start to the data date (in progress) or to the actual finish (complete)
Schedule forecast A prediction of future schedule conditions based on current progress and trends; reissued as work performance data arrive
Schedule network diagram A graphic of the logical relationships (dependencies) among activities
Critical path The longest path through the network; it determines the shortest possible project duration and normally has zero total float
Float (total, free, negative) Total float: delay possible without delaying the finish date or violating a constraint. Free float: delay possible without delaying the early start of a successor. Negative float: constraints force dates earlier than the logic and durations allow
Lead / lag Lead: a successor can start earlier than the logic implies. Lag: a successor is delayed. Durations never include them
Critical chain A schedule method that places buffers on any path to account for limited resources and uncertainty (CCPM aggregates task buffers into a project buffer)
Schedule reserve (buffer) Time added to protect the finish date from identified uncertainty, kept visible rather than hidden in estimates
Timebox / iteration / sprint / release Timebox: a short, fixed period. Iteration (sprint): a timeboxed cycle that produces a usable increment, typically 2 weeks to a month. Release: components put into production together (often 3 to 6 months of work)
Velocity The team's rate of producing deliverables that are validated and accepted within a fixed interval
Story point A unit for the relative effort needed for a user story
Schedule flexibility The ability to adapt to change, manage risk and optimize resources; supports incremental delivery and morale

2The Three Schedule Processes

Process Focus area Purpose Key outputs Decision tools
Plan Schedule Management Planning Set policies, procedures and documentation for designing, developing, managing and maintaining the schedule Schedule management plan Expert judgment, alternative analysis, meetings
Develop Schedule Planning (iterative) Analyze sequences, durations, resource needs and constraints to create the schedule model; may require revising estimates, resources and reserves before approval as the baseline Schedule baseline, project schedule, schedule data, project calendars, change requests Decomposition, rolling wave planning, precedence diagramming, leads and lags, dependency determination, estimating, reserve analysis, what-if, simulation, schedule network analysis, schedule compression, critical path / critical chain, resource optimization, agile release planning
Monitor and Control Schedule Monitoring & Controlling Track status, update the schedule, manage changes to the baseline or agreed schedule, and keep it realistic Work performance information, schedule forecasts, change requests, plan and document updates Earned value, burnup/burndown charts, trend and variance analysis, performance reviews, what-if, critical path, schedule compression, velocity, daily coordination meetings, sprint reviews, backlog refinement

3Plan Schedule Management

The schedule management plan is formal or informal, broad or detailed, and defines the criteria and activities for developing, monitoring and controlling the schedule. It sets:

Element What it defines
Schedule model development The scheduling method and tool
Release and iteration length Timeboxes for releases, waves and iterations (adaptive). Timeboxing minimizes scope creep by forcing essential features first
Level of accuracy The acceptable range for duration estimates, possibly including contingency
Units of measure Staff hours, days, weeks; quantities
Links to the WBS and organizational procedures The WBS is the framework for schedule and estimates
Schedule model maintenance How status and progress are recorded
Control thresholds Variance limits (usually % deviations from the baseline) that trigger action
Rules of performance measurement Percent-complete rules, EVM techniques, SV and SPI
Reporting formats Format and frequency of schedule reports

ECO: prepare a schedule based on the selected development approach. Predictive: define the schedule up front with milestones, dependencies and critical paths. Adaptive: timeboxed schedules with short planning horizons that absorb scope and priority change. Hybrid: predictive milestones at the top; adaptive sprints for fast-changing components; other components may use Kanban or the critical path method (Section 8).

4Develop Schedule: the Four Steps

Step 1: Define activities

Decompose work packages into schedule activities that can be estimated, scheduled, executed and controlled. Outputs: activity list, activity attributes, milestones. Where detail is not yet known, plan the near term in detail and the far term at a higher level (rolling wave; Topic 14).

Step 2: Determine sequence

  • Every activity except the first and last needs at least one predecessor and one successor, with an appropriate logical relationship.
  • Leads and lags make the schedule realistic but must not replace schedule logic; document them. Avoid multiple relationships between the same two activities and closed loops.
Relationship Driving dates With a lag (a lead is a negative lag) Example: predecessor runs from day 5 to day 12
Finish-to-start (FS) Predecessor finish drives successor start Successor start ≥ predecessor finish + lag FS + 3: successor can start on day 15
Start-to-start (SS) Predecessor start drives successor start Successor start ≥ predecessor start + lag SS + 2: successor can start on day 7
Finish-to-finish (FF) Predecessor finish drives successor finish Successor finish ≥ predecessor finish + lag FF + 4: successor can finish on day 16
Start-to-finish (SF) Predecessor start drives successor finish Successor finish ≥ predecessor start + lag SF + 6: successor can finish on day 11

The example adds the lag to the date, as many practice items do. If the network counts days from 1 (the PMBOK 8 convention, Topic 34), an FS successor starts the day after the predecessor finishes, so check which convention the item uses. FS is the most common; SF is rare. Mandatory, discretionary, internal and external classify why a dependency exists; they are not logical relationships.

  • Sequencing can be done at the control account, work package or activity level.
  • Path convergence (several predecessors) and divergence (several successors) carry more risk because the activity is affected by, or affects, several others.
  • Each dependency is mandatory or discretionary and internal or external. Document discretionary ones: they create arbitrary float and limit options later (Topic 14 section 9). External dependencies must be coordinated and shown, not assumed away.

Step 3: Estimate effort and duration

Estimates come from the people most familiar with the work, using resource calendars and the estimated resources. PMBOK 8 techniques: expert judgment, Delphi, analogous, parametric, PERT, bottom-up, planning poker, story points, T-shirt sizing (formulas and use in Topic 14, section 8).

Factor to consider Note
Fixed duration, effort or resource count Some work takes a set time regardless of resources (a 24-hour stress test)
Number of resources Doubling resources does not halve the duration; beyond a point more people add knowledge transfer, learning curves and coordination
Law of diminishing returns Adding one factor while others stay fixed eventually yields smaller gains
Technology advances New equipment can change duration and resource needs
Level of decomposition Estimates at control account, work package or activity level
Documentation Record all assumptions and data behind each duration estimate
Cognitive bias Planning fallacy, end-of-story illusion, Hofstadter's law and motivation affect accuracy
Data quality Estimates are progressively elaborated as better data arrive

Benchmarks and historical data (ECO enabler): reviewing historical information supports analogous and parametric estimates. Such models are reliable when the historical data are accurate, the parameters are quantifiable and the model is scalable (works for large and small projects and for phases). Benchmarking against comparable organizations gives good practices and reference values. Lessons learned from similar earlier projects should shape the plan; they identify the specific causes of earlier delays, which a generic buffer does not address.

Step 4: Adjust

Review the draft schedule. If it is unacceptable, apply schedule compression, resource optimization, reserves or alternative logic (section 5). The team confirms that dates do not clash with resource calendars or assignments in other projects. Analyze logic conflicts and the need for resource leveling, involve stakeholders, then approve and baseline the schedule.

5Schedule Network Analysis

5.1 Critical path method (CPM)

Concept Rule
Forward pass Early start (ES) and early finish (EF) from the start. PMBOK 8 uses the day-1 convention: EF = ES + duration − 1
Backward pass Late finish (LF) and late start (LS) from the end: LS = LF − duration + 1
Total float LS − ES, equivalently LF − EF (identical under either convention)
Free float Day-1 convention: ES (successor) − EF − 1; older convention: ES (successor) − EF
Critical path The longest path; zero total float (the lowest float if a constraint is imposed)
Near-critical paths Many networks have several; watch them
Negative float Constraints demand dates earlier than the logic allows; analyze it to find how much acceleration is needed

CPM ignores resource limits; its dates are time windows within which activities may run, not the final schedule. Critical path drag (PMBOK 8) is how much time a critical activity adds to the project: the maximum it can be shortened before it stops being critical.

5.2 Schedule compression and resource optimization

Technique What changes Cost / risk Applies to
Crashing Add resources (overtime, extra people, expedited delivery) Higher cost; may not produce a viable result Critical-path activities that more resources actually shorten
Fast tracking Do in parallel what was planned in sequence Rework, quality risk, coordination effort, possibly cost Critical-path activities that can overlap
Resource leveling Move dates to balance demand with supply May change the critical path and delay the end date Over-allocated or limited shared resources
Resource smoothing Use free and total float only Critical path and end date unchanged; may not solve every peak Over-allocated resources on activities with float

Compression shortens the schedule without reducing scope, and only compression of critical-path activities shortens the finish date.

5.3 Other analysis tools

  • Critical chain method (CCPM): based on the theory of constraints. Task-level buffers are replaced by one project buffer (and feeding buffers) on a resource-leveled critical path; the buffer protection index compares buffer consumed with chain progress, giving an early warning for the due date.
  • What-if scenario analysis: compute schedules under scenarios such as a late delivery, a strike or a permit change; use the results to size reserves and prepare response plans.
  • Simulation (Monte Carlo): probability of meeting a date (Topic 21).
  • Reserve analysis: are the schedule and budget reserves sufficient for the remaining risk?
  • Aggregating reserves where paths converge or diverge reduces slip probability; review the critical path for high-risk or long-lead items.
  • Branch and bound (PMBOK 8): an optimization method that prunes poor schedule sequences to find one that minimizes duration within constraints.

5.4 Schedule baseline

After conflicts are resolved and stakeholders approve, the schedule model becomes the schedule baseline (baseline start and finish dates). The working project schedule is then updated with actuals and forecasts while the baseline stays fixed. Together with the scope and cost baselines it forms the performance measurement baseline. Changes to the baseline, including corrections of errors, go through change control (Topic 29). Approved changes must also be reflected in the schedule and related documents.

6Coordinate With Other Projects and Operations (ECO enabler)

PMBOK 8 treats interdependencies (reliance on other projects, departments or functions for decisions, components or resources) as a factor in the approach, and asks team members to confirm that dates do not conflict with resource calendars or assignments in other projects.

Area Actions
External dependencies Permits, utility connections, other projects' deliverables: identify them, agree dates with the owners, show them as external milestones or constraints, track them as risks
Shared resources Check calendars and competing assignments; agree release dates with the functional managers or the PMO (Topic 19)
Operations constraints Beyond PMBOK 8 Change-freeze windows, peak seasons, maintenance windows, shift patterns, outage approvals: build them into the schedule as constraints
Program and portfolio Coordinate through the program, portfolio or PMO; align release dates and interfaces
Governance Escalate conflicts that exceed your authority (Topic 12); keep stakeholders informed (Topic 20)

7Agile and Hybrid Scheduling

(Planning layers, burn charts and Kanban are illustrated in Topic 04.)

  • Release planning: a high-level summary timeline of the release schedule (typically 3 to 6 months) from the product roadmap and vision; it fixes the number of iterations; features show what value arrives when.
  • Iteration plan: a detailed plan for the current iteration (a timebox, typically 2 weeks to a month): tasks estimated in hours inside iteration planning, stories in story points.
  • Velocity is the rate at which work is produced, validated and accepted per iteration. Forecast: remaining backlog ÷ velocity = iterations remaining Beyond PMBOK 8formula. Example: 120 points ÷ 24 points = 5 iterations (10 weeks at 2 weeks each). Use a range of velocities for a range of dates, and refine as data accumulate.
  • Burnup chart: work completed toward a milestone against the total scope line (shows scope growth and progress). Burndown chart: work remaining versus time left in a timebox, with an ideal line and a forecast trend. A burnup showing scope rising as fast as work completes means the team is delivering steadily while scope grows; it is not a sign the team is slowing.
  • Backlog refinement keeps the next iterations ready; the daily coordination meeting and sprint review are the control mechanisms.
  • Fix time and cost, flex scope: deliver prioritized increments; the iteration length does not stretch to absorb unfinished work.
  • Hybrid: executives see milestones with iteration plans beneath them. A detailed Gantt built from the backlog adds false precision. Some streams may use Kanban or the critical path method.
  • Other approaches (PMBOK 8): location-based scheduling (quantities allocated to locations, production rates, crew sizes), lean scheduling (pull planning: master scheduling, phase scheduling, look-ahead planning; work pulled when capacity exists), the Last Planner System, Gantt charts and Kanban. Keep each WBS element's schedule at a commensurate level of detail.
  • Velocity is output, not value: steady velocity does not prove value delivered; check outcomes with stakeholders.

8Monitor and Control Schedule (and Analyze Variation)

Predictive (PMBOK 8): determine schedule status; influence the factors that cause change; reconsider reserves; decide whether the overall schedule has changed; manage actual changes. Any change to the baseline or agreed schedule is approved through Assess and Implement Changes (integrated change control).

Adaptive: compare work delivered and accepted with the estimates for the elapsed cycle; hold retrospectives; reprioritize the backlog; track velocity; manage changes as they occur.

Contracted work: regular and milestone status updates from contractors, plus status reviews and walkthroughs, confirm the supplier's reports are accurate and complete.

Analyze schedule variation (ECO enabler):

Measure Formula Reading
Schedule variance (SV) EV − PV Negative: behind the plan
Schedule performance index (SPI) EV ÷ PV Below 1: behind; above 1: ahead
Variance analysis Baseline vs actual: cause and degree Review time, cost, technical and resource variances together
Trend analysis Project future results from history Early warning of slippage

(Earned value calculations are in Topic 34 and reporting in Topic 28.)

Response sequence for a variance:

  1. Find the cause (root cause analysis).
  2. Check the effect on the critical path and float. An SPI below 1 on work with large float may not threaten the finish date; delay on the critical path does. Beyond PMBOK 8
  3. Evaluate options: crash, fast track, re-sequence, use or reassess reserves, reduce scope through change control, escalate if beyond authority.
  4. Use change control when the baseline would change; update schedule, forecasts and documents; communicate to stakeholders.
  5. Re-check the forecast; keep the schedule realistic throughout.

9Predictive vs Agile vs Hybrid

Predictive Agile / adaptive Hybrid
Schedule form Detailed schedule with baseline, network and critical path Roadmap, release plan, iteration plans (timeboxes) Milestone schedule on top; iterations or Kanban beneath
Planning Up front; progressive elaboration within phases Just enough, replanned each iteration Predictive for the envelope, adaptive for details
Estimating Parametric, bottom-up, three-point; effort converted to durations Story points, velocity; team estimates Both
Control Baseline vs actual; SV, SPI; change control for baseline changes Delivered and accepted work vs plan; velocity; burn charts; backlog reprioritization Milestones tracked formally; iterations by burn charts
Flex Fix scope, control change Fix time and cost, flex scope Fix milestones and date, flex content
Tools CPM, resource optimization, crashing, fast tracking Timeboxing, backlog refinement, daily coordination, retrospectives Both
Beyond PMBOK 8 Velocity-range forecasting

10Tailoring, Interactions and Checking Results

Tailoring considerations (PMBOK 8 §2.3.3):

Factor Effect
Life cycle and approach Predictive: detailed, baselined, comprehensive milestones and critical paths. Adaptive: flexible timeboxed schedules. Hybrid: predictive milestones with adaptive or Kanban/CPM streams
Product and deliverable High criticality or compliance means more detailed, more frequent updates; new technology means more iterative scheduling
Team Large or dispersed teams need better tools and more frequent updates; experienced teams can use a higher-level schedule
Culture Adaptive cultures tolerate fluid schedules; risk-averse ones prefer detailed, fixed schedules; high trust and buy-in permit flexibility
Environment Megaprojects need more detail than small ones; aggressive timelines need more rigor
Methods CPM, critical chain, location-based scheduling, Last Planner System, Gantt, Kanban, lean scheduling

Interactions: scope, schedule and finance are tightly linked; duration depends on scope, cost, resources and quality. Governance controls changes; risk drives reserves; stakeholders must take part in building the schedule; resources set feasibility.

Check results (Table 2-7):

Outcome Check
Scheduling approach fits the deliverables Schedule aligned with the development approach
Life cycle connects value delivery Phases from launch to close with exit criteria
Holistic delivery schedule No gaps or misalignments
Schedule documentation complete Dependencies, durations, resources, milestones
Tools and techniques used For example project management software and CPM
Stakeholders involved Low involvement leads to an unrealistic schedule
Buffers for known-unknowns Floats, contingency reserves or alternate network strategies such as secondary plans

11Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

  1. Only critical-path compression shortens the finish date. Do not add resources to a non-critical activity to recover a late project.
  2. Crashing costs money; fast tracking adds risk and rework. Neither cuts scope. Pick by cost and risk, and use change control if the baseline changes.
  3. Smooth within float first. Over-allocation on non-critical work is solved by resource smoothing at no cost; leveling can move the end date.
  4. Total float vs free float: total float is shared along a path; free float is the delay that does not disturb the next activity.
  5. More people do not shorten work in proportion. Consider diminishing returns, ramp-up and coordination.
  6. Padding is not a reserve. Keep schedule reserves explicit and tied to risk (Topics 14 and 21).
  7. Estimates come from the people doing the work and carry documented assumptions. Benchmarks and historical data support, not replace, them.
  8. External dependencies and operations constraints belong in the schedule and are coordinated with their owners; do not assume standard timelines.
  9. Baseline changes, even corrections of errors, go through change control; approved changes must be reflected in the schedule and documents.
  10. Hybrid view for executives: milestones with iterations beneath; do not convert a backlog into a detailed Gantt.
  11. Agile: fix the timebox, flex the scope. Route new work through the backlog; do not stretch iterations.
  12. A burnup that shows scope growth is not a slow team. Explain the data; do not push for speed.
  13. SPI or SV is not the whole story: analyze the critical path and float before deciding the end date is at risk; velocity is output, not value.
  14. Use lessons learned from similar projects to shape the plan; do not add a generic buffer.
  15. When two stakeholders expect different dates, facilitate agreement rather than analyzing both dates in more depth.
  16. Involve stakeholders and the team in building the schedule; low involvement produces unrealistic schedules.
  17. Use relative sizing for uncertain agile work instead of padding hour estimates.

12Exam Q&A

12.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1In a network, Design (3 days) precedes Build (5 days) and Procure (4 days), and both Build and Procure precede Install (2 days). How much total float does Procure have?

  • ANone, because Procure starts at the same time as the critical Build
  • BOne day, because the path through Build is one day longer
  • CTwo days, because Install is shorter than both Build and Procure
  • DThree days, because Procure is shorter than the first activity, Design
Show the answer

Answer: B. The path through Build takes 10 days and is critical, while the path through Procure takes 9, so Procure can slip one day without delaying the finish. Starting at the same time as Build gives Procure no float by itself, and the durations of Install and Design do not decide it.

S2A team has 150 story points left, and its last four sprints delivered 25, 30, 30 and 35 points. About how many more sprints should the project manager forecast?

  • A5 to 6 sprints, from the 25 to 35 point velocity range, rounded up
  • B2 sprints, using the 120-point total of the four sprints as one sprint's velocity
  • C4 sprints, using only the best sprint and rounding the result down
  • D10 sprints, halving the velocity to allow a safety margin for the team
Show the answer

Answer: A. Remaining backlog divided by velocity gives the sprints left: 150 divided by 35 is about 4.3 and 150 divided by 25 is 6, so a range of 5 to 6 sprints after rounding up. Using a cumulative total, only the best sprint or an arbitrary halving distorts the forecast.

S3Resource leveling of over-allocated electricians moved two critical activities and pushed the end date out by two weeks, but the sponsor insists on the original date. What should the project manager do next?

  • ATell the sponsor that the new end date is unavoidable and cannot be changed
  • BReverse the leveling and accept the electricians' overallocation to protect the date
  • CSmooth the resources using float, which will restore the original end date
  • DEvaluate crashing or fast tracking and present the options for approval
Show the answer

Answer: D. Leveling can change the critical path and delay the end date, so to recover time without reducing scope the project manager evaluates crashing or fast tracking and takes the options, with their costs and risks, through change control. Reversing the leveling, declaring the date fixed or smoothing (which cannot fix critical activities) does not address the date.

S4Poured concrete must cure for three days before the steel frame can be erected. How should this be shown in the schedule network?

  • AAs a finish-to-start relationship with a three-day lag
  • BAs a start-to-start relationship with no lag between the two activities
  • CAs a finish-to-start relationship with a three-day lead between the activities
  • DBy adding three days to the duration of the concrete pouring activity
Show the answer

Answer: A. A lag delays the successor, so waiting for concrete to cure is a finish-to-start relationship with a lag, while a lead would let the frame start earlier. Durations never include leads or lags, and start-to-start logic misrepresents the dependency.

S5On a critical chain schedule, 60% of the project buffer has been consumed while only 20% of the chain is complete. What does this signal?

  • AAn early warning that the due date is at risk, so recovery actions should be prepared
  • BA sign that the task estimates were too low and should now be rewritten
  • CA reason to remove the buffer and reallocate its time to the individual tasks
  • DNothing yet, because buffers are meant to be consumed over the life of the project
Show the answer

Answer: A. The buffer protection index compares buffer consumed with chain progress, so heavy consumption at low progress warns that the due date is threatened. Treating consumption as normal, removing the buffer or rewriting estimates ignores the warning.

S6To halve the time to deliver a feature set that needs four sprints, the sponsor asks the project manager to double the number of developers. What is the best response?

  • ADouble the team and halve the estimate in the baseline immediately
  • BExplain that adding people does not halve duration, and assess the real effect first
  • CDouble the team, because duration always falls in proportion to the resources added
  • DReject the request, since adding resources never shortens any activity at all
Show the answer

Answer: B. More people add learning curves and coordination, so duration does not fall in proportion, although some activities do benefit. The project manager assesses the real effect rather than accepting proportional savings, refusing outright or rewriting the baseline.

S7A work package has an SPI of 0.85, but it has 20 days of total float and is not on the critical path. The sponsor demands immediate crashing. What should the project manager do first?

  • AFast-track the whole project to offset the delay on the work package
  • BCrash the work package at once, since an SPI below 1 always demands action
  • CCheck the effect on the critical path and float before deciding on action
  • DIgnore the variance entirely because the work sits on a path with float
Show the answer

Answer: C. A poor SPI on work with ample float may not threaten the finish date, so the project manager finds the cause and checks the effect on the critical path before choosing a response. Crashing automatically, ignoring the variance or fast tracking everything skips that analysis.

S8A highway project repeats the same tasks along twelve 1-km segments, and crews idle while waiting for the previous segment. Which scheduling approach suits the repeated work best?

  • AResource smoothing, which moves tasks into their float without moving the end date
  • BVelocity-based forecasting, which divides the backlog by the team's story points
  • CCritical chain scheduling, which gathers all of the float into a single buffer
  • DLocation-based scheduling, using production rates and crew sizes for each segment
Show the answer

Answer: D. Location-based scheduling allocates quantities to locations using production rates and crew sizes, so crews flow from segment to segment without waiting. The other techniques address buffers, backlogs or float, not repeated work along a line.

S9A strike at the port might delay the arrival of key equipment, and the project manager wants to know how that would affect the finish date and how much reserve to hold. Which technique helps?

  • ACrashing, paying for overtime on every activity after the equipment arrives
  • BFast tracking, overlapping the activities that follow the equipment arrival
  • CWhat-if scenario analysis for the strike and no-strike cases
  • DResource leveling, moving the activities until the demand for labor is even
Show the answer

Answer: C. What-if scenario analysis computes the schedule under scenarios such as a late delivery or a strike, and the results size reserves and prepare responses. Leveling, fast tracking and crashing change the plan rather than test its exposure.

S10To recover one day, the project manager can crash activity X (critical, 2,000 per day), activity Y (critical, 1,500 per day) or activity Z (not critical, 500 per day). Which should be crashed?

  • AActivity X, because it is the first critical activity in the network
  • BActivity Y, the cheapest critical-path activity to shorten
  • CAll three activities, so that the savings are spread across the schedule
  • DActivity Z, because it has the lowest cost per day of shortening the work
Show the answer

Answer: B. Only compressing critical-path activities shortens the finish date, and among those the cheapest per day is chosen first. Z is cheap but changes nothing, X costs more than Y, and crashing all three wastes money.

12.2 Recall Q&As

R1Name the three Schedule processes.

Show the answer

Plan Schedule Management, Develop Schedule, Monitor and Control Schedule.

R2What are the four steps of Develop Schedule?

Show the answer

Define activities, determine sequence, estimate effort and duration, adjust.

R3What does the schedule management plan define?

Show the answer

Schedule model method and tool, release and iteration length, level of accuracy, units of measure, WBS and organizational links, model maintenance, control thresholds, performance measurement rules (EVM), reporting formats.

R4Effort versus duration?

Show the answer

Effort is labor units required; duration is the number of work periods needed with the assigned resources and calendars.

R5Name the four logical relationships.

Show the answer

Finish-to-start (most common), start-to-start, finish-to-finish and start-to-finish (very rare).

R6Lead versus lag?

Show the answer

A lead lets a successor start earlier than the logic implies (negative lag); a lag delays it. Durations do not include either, and they must not replace logic.

R7What is the critical path?

Show the answer

The longest path, which sets the shortest possible project duration; normally zero total float.

R8Total float versus free float?

Show the answer

Total float is the delay possible without delaying the project end or violating a constraint; free float is the delay possible without delaying a successor's early start.

R9Crashing versus fast tracking?

Show the answer

Crashing adds resources to shorten critical activities at extra cost; fast tracking overlaps activities normally done in sequence, risking rework.

R10Resource leveling versus smoothing?

Show the answer

Leveling balances demand and supply by moving dates and may change the critical path and end date; smoothing uses float only and leaves both unchanged.

R11What is the critical chain method?

Show the answer

A method that places buffers (a project buffer instead of task buffers in CCPM) on a resource-leveled critical path to protect the due date, tracked with the buffer protection index.

R12What is velocity, and what do burnup and burndown charts show?

Show the answer

Velocity is accepted work produced per iteration. A burnup chart shows work done against total scope over time; a burndown chart shows work remaining against time left.

R13Give the SV and SPI formulas.

Show the answer

SV = EV − PV; SPI = EV ÷ PV.

R14Schedule model, project schedule and schedule baseline?

Show the answer

The model is the representation used to compute the schedule; the project schedule is its output with dates, durations and resources; the baseline is the approved version of the schedule model, changed only through change control.

13Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Processes Plan Schedule Mgmt → Develop Schedule (4 steps) → Monitor and Control Schedule
Four steps Define activities → Determine sequence → Estimate effort and duration → Adjust
Schedule management plan Method, tool, release and iteration length, accuracy, units, maintenance, thresholds, measurement rules, reports
Relationships FS (common), SS, FF, SF (rare); leads and lags do not replace logic
Dependencies Mandatory/discretionary; internal/external; document discretionary; coordinate external
Estimating PMBOK 8 lists expert, Delphi, analogous, parametric, PERT, bottom-up, planning poker, story points, T-shirt sizing
Resources and duration More people do not cut duration in proportion
CPM Longest path = shortest duration; EF = ES + D − 1 and LS = LF − D + 1 (day-1 convention)
Float Total = LS − ES = LF − EF; free float = ES(next) − EF − 1; negative float = constraint violated
Compression Crashing (cost) and fast tracking (risk), critical path only, scope unchanged
Resource optimization Leveling (may delay end, may change critical path) vs smoothing (float only)
Critical chain Buffers on a resource-leveled chain; project buffer; buffer protection index
